title: Look for Passionate Advocates When Consensus Is Impossible
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This brief Admired Leadership piece offers a decision rule for teams that cannot reach consensus. It affirms that consensus builds goodwill and buy-in, but recognizes that strong-minded colleagues sometimes disagree, and it rejects defaulting to a unilateral call. The author's move is to listen for passion rather than tally positions: because rejecting a decision is always easier, passionate support should outweigh passionate opposition. The threshold is a quorum of at least two committed advocates; without them, the leader should keep the issue open and delay. An E.M. Forster line anchors the argument that one passionate person outweighs many who are merely interested.
points: When consensus fails, leaders need an alternative path that avoids simply making the call unilaterally.
Because it is always easier to dispute a decision, the author argues that passionately in favor should overrule passionately against.
The practical threshold is a quorum of two or more passionate advocates; lacking that, the decision should be delayed rather than forced.
quotes: Consensus fosters goodwill for future decisions, as well as ensuring the buy-in so critical to executing or implementing the decision. But smart and strong-minded colleagues sometimes disagree.
But the best leaders always listen for passion around a decision. They look to see who feels the need to champion the idea.

Tuning into the frequency of passion helps leaders sort out where the whole team really stands on a decision. Because it is always easier to dispute or reject a decision, passionately in favor should always overrule passionately against.

When consensus is negated, identifying two or more passionate advocates lights the pathway forward. With anything less than a core group of zealots in favor of the decision, good leaders should share the discomfort of those against the decision and keep the issue on the table until a different solution or choice presents itself.
Passionate advocates tip the scales when consensus can’t be reached. Find them, or mark time until you do.
